headline: East end on the 5:41 ebb: bluefish stacked, bass still playing coy
subhead: The moon's building toward full and the current's tightening up the bite windows on both ends of the ditch — the blues are all in, the bass are still feeling it out.
body_markdown:
Max ebb at the east end ran right around 5:41 this week, and for the last ninety minutes of that stage the water off Sandwich was doing exactly what it's supposed to do in early September — stacking bait against the rip and turning bluefish into a chopping machine. That's been the story on both ends of the Canal for the better part of ten days now: the ebb is the tide to fish, the blues are eating everything that moves, and the bass are around in real numbers but still playing the coy game they've been playing since the water sat in the low 70s through August.

We flagged this last week — said the building moon would tighten current strength and sharpen the bite windows through the Canal — and that's exactly what's happened. With the moon pushing toward full on the 6th and 7th, the current at both ends has picked up noticeably off the neap lull from ten days back. Max ebb and max flood are both running harder, the rip lines are holding shape longer instead of collapsing into slop, and that extra push is exactly the kind of current that turns bait-holding water into feeding water. The next 48 to 72 hours should only sharpen that further as the moon tops out.

East end remains the show. The rip off the power plant and the stretch down toward the Sandwich side of the canal mouth have had bluefish stacked on peanut bunker and mackerel schools pushing through on the last two hours of the ebb, right into the top of slack. Boats and shore guys working that window with Ava 27s and 47s, tins like Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters in the 2- to 3-ounce range, and topwater poppers during the last hour of light have had steady action — blues to 8 and 9 pounds, some genuine chopper-class fish mixed in, and that bite has held up better than the bass bite for most of the week. Striped bass are in that same water, but they're not committing the way the blues are. Best luck on bass has come to guys slowing down — bucktails in white or chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounce, bounced along bottom on the last of the ebb, or a tube-and-worm trolled slow through the seam where the rip meets the flat water. Fish have been mostly schoolie-to-mid-20s class, with the occasional better fish, but nobody's calling it a blitz yet.

West end tells a similar story with different scenery. The current seams off Mashnee Island and around Hog Island have been the go-to for guys chasing bass on the flood, particularly the middle two hours when the seam sets up clean and holds bait against the edge instead of blowing it through. Wings Neck and the mouth of Phinneys Harbor have had some quality fluke still coming off sandy bottom on Gulp in white and pink, 3- to 4-inch paddletails on light jigheads, though that bite is thinning out fast the way it does every year this time — doormats are already sliding toward deeper structure outside, and what's left inside is mostly keeper-class fish, not the numbers game July and August gave up. If fluke is the target, the west end drift on the last of the incoming, working slow along the drop where the channel meets the flat, is still worth the trip, just don't expect it to last much past the middle of the month.

Bait-wise, the canal's getting a healthy push of peanut bunker and mackerel through both ends right now, which is exactly what's holding the bluefish so tight to the rips. Striped bass are clearly feeding on that same bait — you can see it in the marks and in the fish that are coming up — but the water hasn't cooled enough yet to flip them from scattered feeders into the kind of tight, aggressive schools that blitz on top. That's consistent with what's happening basin-wide right now: bunker schools building in the bays and sounds to the south still need a real cool-down to trigger that switch, and the Canal usually follows that same clock, just compressed because the current does half the work for the fish that the bays have to do with water temperature alone.

No albacore or bonito reports worth hanging a hat on inside the Canal itself yet — that push is still working its way west through the Sound and Buzzards Bay approaches, and if it reaches the west end mouth in the next week or two, expect it to show first around Wings Neck and the outer edge of Phinneys Harbor where clean water meets the current. Worth keeping small profile epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks in the bag on the off chance a pod shows on the surface near the west end breakwater.

Looking ahead, the building moon through the weekend should keep tightening these bite windows — expect max current speeds a touch stronger each day through the 7th, which means the rip lines will hold their shape longer and the feeding windows around slack will be shorter but more concentrated. If there's only one tide to fish this week, make it the evening ebb at the east end — that's where the bait's thickest and the current's doing the most work. West end guys should target the flood's middle two hours around Mashnee for the better bass shots. If overnight temps start dropping the way the calendar suggests they should, the first real bass commitment of the fall could show up in the Canal within the next week to ten days — right on the heels of whatever breaks loose in the bays to the south.
